messages.subject: Mixture models with multiple assignments per mixture
parts:
Hi,

I would like to ask for some model guidance. I apologise in advance if my problem seems trivial, but my experience with Bayesian models is limited.

I am trying to identify mixtures in a population, in which each data point has its own profile. The tricky part is that each data point may be a member of multiple mixtures. From what I have found so far, this can be modelled using the so-called "Indian Buffet Process" (IBP) (Griffiths et al., 2011). However, as I have been able to read in the reference and on the board, Stan does not (yet) handle these kind of infinite models. From other threads on this forum, I have seen people have been mimicking the Chinese Restaurant Process using a very large number of mixtures. Can, or have, something similar been done for the IBP?

I am not even sure this is the best model to use, but I do not know of any better. To go a bit more into detail, the data is a NxM matrix, in which there are N data points and M measurements. The measurements are continous and (approximately) normally distributed (on log scale). Each data point has a lot of measurements with a zero value, simply because nothing was detected.

I have tried to come up with a complete description, but if anything is missing, please do ask!

Thanks in advance.

Cheers,
David

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Mixture models with multiple assignments per mixture
parts:
Trivial's a matter of perspective --- almost everything's
hard the first time and trivial after the tenth time.

It doesn't sound like you have an infinite mixture if you have
a fixed number of columns. From Griffith's and Gharamani's
abstract ( https://cocosci.berkeley.edu/tom/papers/indianbuffet.pdf ):

The Indian buffet process is a stochastic process defining
a probability distribution over equiva- lence classes of sparse
binary matrices with a finite number of rows and an unbounded number
of columns. This distribution is suitable for use as a prior
in probabilistic models that represent objects using a potentially
infinite array of features, or that involve bipartite graphs in
which the size of at least one class of nodes is unknown.

The thing to do when building a Bayesian model is to consider how
the data is generated (here it sounds like some kind of measurement
process). Could you say a bit more about what the
colummns are and how the zero entries come about if the measurements
are approximately lognormal (0 isn't going to come out of a lognormal
observation)? For example, is it a censoring process that truncates
low measurements to zero? If so, you probably just want a model to
account for the censoring. Is there any relation among the columns
or are they all different kinds of measurements?

- Bob

parts:
It could be me that read it wrong. I was thinking of it as mixture model with an infinite number of mixtures, in which each data point could be member of multiple mixtures. 

Yes, it is indeed a measurement process. Each "feature" is the same measurement, measured under slightly different conditions. What we expect is that feature 1 is correlated to feature 2, and feature 2 to 3, ..., approximately until we measure 0 (absence). The standard in my field is to work with log-values, so I use the log(value+1) transformation to avoid the log(0) errors, and this is (approximately) normally distributed, excluding the 0 measurements. 

To give an example:

A = [4.5, 5, 6, 5.5, 8, 0, 0, 0, 0, 3, 2.3, 4.5]
B = [4.5, 5, 6, 5.5, 8, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]
C = [0, 0, , 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 2.9, 2.2, 4.4]

So A would have the profile [4.5, 5, 6] and [3, 2.3, 4.5]. What I would like to identify is that point A has two mixtures (1 and 2), B has one mixture (1) and C has one mixture (2). Thus mixture 1 consists of A+B, and mixture 2 consists of A+C.

I hope the explanation was clear. 

Cheers,
David

parts:
> On Mar 4, 2015, at 12:01 AM, David Westergaard <da...@harsk.dk> wrote:
>
> It could be me that read it wrong. I was thinking of it as mixture model with an infinite number of mixtures, in which each data point could be member of multiple mixtures.

It's for infinitely fat mixtures. If you have finitely
many columns and model each one, then there's only finitely
many. It's the "unbounded number of columns" part that
your data's missing.

> Yes, it is indeed a measurement process. Each "feature" is the same measurement, measured under slightly different conditions. What we expect is that feature 1 is correlated to feature 2, and feature 2 to 3, ..., approximately until we measure 0 (absence).

It would probably help if you could be more specific (less abstract)
about what these measurements are.

A mixture would indeed give you that correlation.

> The standard in my field is to work with log-values, so I use the log(value+1) transformation to avoid the log(0) errors, and this is (approximately) normally distributed, excluding the 0 measurements.
>
> To give an example:
>
> A = [4.5, 5, 6, 5.5, 8, 0, 0, 0, 0, 3, 2.3, 4.5]
> B = [4.5, 5, 6, 5.5, 8, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]
> C = [0, 0, , 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 2.9, 2.2, 4.4]
>
> So A would have the profile [4.5, 5, 6] and [3, 2.3, 4.5].

Is that the result of log(measurement + 1) or the raw measurements
that you'll add 1 to and take the log?

Is there some physical correspondence to a profile here?
> What I would like to identify is that point A has two mixtures (1 and 2), B has one mixture (1) and C has one mixture (2). Thus mixture 1 consists of A+B, and mixture 2 consists of A+C.

Does the order of the columns matter? For instance, are
they measurements over time? Clearly the behavior isn't
continuous, because you go from 8 down to 0 in one step. But
the values close to each other look related in A. That would
matter in terms of how you'd want to model it.

Then the question is what do you expect the relationship to
be between A's and B's measurement. It looks like B has
one of the components of A and C has one of the components
of A.

If so, you might want something like a change point
time-series model. The data for A is probably three mixtures,
if you include the zeroes. You want to model the entire
data generating process, including generating the zeroes.

So a simple model might assume some number of mixture components K,
each with means mu[k] and std devs sigma[k], and then each
row would start in one of the comonents, continue to draw from
that mixture for some number of observations, then drop to 0 or
another mixture.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Mixture models with multiple assignments per mixture
parts:
OK, I think I see this a bit better. What you probably want
to be looking at in the way of non-parametrics is a Dirichlet
process prior on the number of mixture components. That would
let the K in my earlier comment be given a prior. If you
have a reasonable upper bound, this can be well approximated with
a finite upper bound on K.

And no, you wouldn't associate each row with a single mixture
component. You'd have something like this for row n:

x[n,1], x[n,2], ..., x[n,M]

and maybe some kind of process for generating a sequence of
components where lambda[n,m] in 1:K is the mixture from which
x[n,m] is drawn,

lambda[n,1], ..., lambda[n,M]

Then you'd want to put a model on how the lambda values transition.
An HMM would be a general way to do it, but they're not very good
at modeling length --- you only get exponential decay beyond a certain
finite memory limit. That's what I was calling the change-point structure.

Thanks for the extra detail on the process --- I'll have to
think a bit more about that. The point's just that you want
to model that process as closely as you can in the statistical
model.

- Bob

prior. Because we don’t handle discrete parameters you’d have
to think about the collapsed IBP, but then you still have to worry
about the unbounded mixture components. As Bob alluded
to in his first email, the only way this will work in Stan is if
you threshold the number of mixture components a priori
and hope that your posterior mass concentrates away from
that threshold.

parts: > This might be a very basic question, but how do I "know" if a component is active? Simply if the probability > 0, or is there a lower-bound that is considered to be ~0 for practical purposes?

You don’t.

When you marginalize out over the mixture components you’re assigning at least some prior
probability to each component which can never be forced exactly to zero. A proper Bayesian
analysis never makes a hard decision to exclude components so there is no canonical way
of trying to impose a “significance” threshold. You have to define a criteria for defining one
yourself.

For example, one criteria might be that for a mixture component to be excluded the posterior
must shrink towards zero relative to the prior. Of course how you define “shrink” and “shrink
enough to be excluded” are open questions.

> I tried to make a simple mixture model in stan (guided mostly by the Stan reference and wikipedia), but right now it is running incredibly slow. After a day it had barely done 25 iterations, so I am guessing it is mixing very poorly for a reason I do not understand. Your model is not implemented correctly — you need to compute the density of each
component and then sum them up for each datum,

real ps[K];

for (k in 1:K) {
ps[k] <- log(theta[k]) + normal_log(y[n], mu[k], sigma[k]);
}

}

Yes, exactly. Except y[n] is is not the count of the places, but the count of the number of proteins in a particular place. In figure 1a from the paper, there are 60 such places. In each of the 60 places, there are either 0 proteins (the protein is not found in the given place or could not be detected), or a number in the billions if the protein is present. Each y[n] thus holds a vector of counts for the given place, so that y[n,m] is the count of protein n in place m.

they get stuck?  To what end?  Are you sure you want to run a Bayesian
model here?

What we want to identify are the proteins that has the same profile / is drawn from the same mixture. If two proteins are co-migrating, they are most likely physically interacting in a complex. At least that is what we hypothesise. The idea running the Bayesian model would be to have priors on the number of mixtures, as well as infer which proteins are co-migrating. It could be there are better ways of doing it, but our initial thought was the Bayesian framework as it is quite flexible.
I don't see how regression is related to clustering.

Definitely, it is not. It was just another approach used in a prior paper.

David

So what I'd do from a Bayesian perspective is calculate the posterior
probability that two proteins, indexed n and n', are from the same
cluster given the observed data, i.e.,

Pr[protein[n] drawn from same cluster as protein[n'] | y]

You can do this with Stan.

The basic idea is that you have the mixture model you have, but
use a lognormal if you are going to log transform, then calculate
the above event probabilities in the generated quantities block:

generated quantities {
matrix[N,N] Pr_same_cluster;

for (m in 1:N)
for (n in (n+1):N)
Pr_same_cluster[m,n] <- pr_same(m,n,y,theta,mu,sigma);
}

For a mixture model, you can calculate using the same ps calculation
you use for the mixture,

log Pr[n in cluster k | y, theta, mu, sigma]

= ps[k] - log_sum_exp(ps)

probabilities, so you need to divide each of the ps[iby the sum, which is another

Sorry for the delayed response! That informational message in ADVI comes up when it has a numerically unstable sample. The default should allow it to drop the point and continue resampling, so don’t worry too much about the informational message. It generally means that either the current initialization is bad (i.e. the informational message happens all the time in the beginning of the procedure), or the model is simply hard to fit.

If the initialization is bad, and there’s no way to fix it on the user end, then I suggest you up the number of grad_samples to make the gradient updates more reliable. Hope this helps.

Dustin

On Tuesday, March 3, 2015 at 6:03:52 AM UTC-5, David Westergaard wrote:
Hi,

I would like to ask for some model guidance. I apologise in advance if my problem seems trivial, but my experience with Bayesian models is limited.

I am trying to identify mixtures in a population, in which each data point has its own profile. The tricky part is that each data point may be a member of multiple mixtures. From what I have found so far, this can be modelled using the so-called "Indian Buffet Process" (IBP) (Griffiths et al., 2011). However, as I have been able to read in the reference and on the board, Stan does not (yet) handle these kind of infinite models.
